reference.source: American Heart Association Scientific Statement on Kawasaki Disease
clinicalPearls: Incomplete Kawasaki disease should be considered in any child with prolonged unexplained fever and fewer than the required number of principal clinical criteria, particularly in infants.
Infants under about six months of age are at highest risk of both incomplete presentation and coronary artery aneurysms, so the threshold for evaluation and treatment should be low.

The principal features may appear sequentially rather than together: bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes with cracked red lips or strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, extremity changes with erythema and oedema followed by periungual peeling, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Supportive laboratory findings — markedly raised inflammatory markers, anaemia, a rising platelet count in the second week, sterile pyuria, transaminitis, hypoalbuminaemia and hyponatraemia — strengthen the diagnosis when clinical criteria are incomplete.
Echocardiography is central: coronary artery dilatation or aneurysm supports the diagnosis and mandates treatment even when full clinical criteria are absent.
Timely immunoglobulin therapy, ideally within the first ten days of illness, substantially reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysms.
Perineal desquamation and erythema or reactivation at a previous BCG scar site are useful supportive clues.
Incomplete Kawasaki disease belongs in the differential of fever of unknown origin and of a prolonged, viral-seeming illness that fails to settle.
reference.pathophysiology: Kawasaki disease is a self-limiting, medium-vessel systemic vasculitis of childhood with a striking predilection for the coronary arteries; the incomplete form shares identical pathology but presents with insufficient clinical criteria to meet the classic case definition. An infectious or environmental trigger is thought to provoke an aberrant, dysregulated immune response in a genetically susceptible child, driving neutrophilic and then mononuclear infiltration of the arterial wall. Inflammation destroys the media and internal elastic lamina, weakening the vessel and predisposing to dilatation and aneurysm formation, most importantly in the coronary tree, where subsequent thrombosis, stenosis or rupture accounts for the principal morbidity and mortality.
additionalDifferentials: Viral exanthems such as measles, adenovirus, enterovirus and Epstein-Barr virus
Streptococcal and staphylococcal toxin-mediated disease, including scarlet fever, toxic shock and scalded skin syndrome
Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome)
Stevens-Johnson syndrome and drug hypersensitivity reactions including DRESS
Other systemic infections such as leptospirosis
additionalInvestigations: Serial echocardiography to assess coronary artery dimensions using body-surface-area-adjusted z-scores
Full blood count showing anaemia and later thrombocytosis, with ESR and CRP
Serum albumin, sodium and liver enzymes
Electrocardiogram for arrhythmia, ischaemia and a baseline recording
Cultures, serology and viral studies to exclude infective mimics
N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide as an adjunctive supportive marker
redFlags: Coronary artery dilatation or aneurysm on echocardiography
Myocarditis, heart failure or circulatory shock (Kawasaki disease shock syndrome)
Persistent or recrudescent fever despite immunoglobulin, indicating treatment resistance
Young infants with prolonged fever and marked irritability
reference.prognosis: With prompt immunoglobulin therapy the great majority of children recover fully, whereas untreated or delayed disease carries a substantial risk of coronary artery aneurysms. Such aneurysms are the leading cause of long-term morbidity and may lead to thrombosis, myocardial ischaemia or sudden death.
pitfalls: Waiting for all classic criteria before treating and thereby delaying immunoglobulin beyond the optimal window
Attributing prolonged fever to a self-limiting viral illness and missing incomplete disease, especially in infants
Being falsely reassured by a normal initial echocardiogram, as coronary changes may evolve later
Overlooking supportive laboratory criteria that would justify treatment
Failing to recognise immunoglobulin resistance requiring escalation of therapy
references: American Heart Association Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-term Management of Kawasaki Disease
management: Give intravenous immunoglobulin as early as possible in the acute illness to reduce the risk of coronary artery aneurysms
Add aspirin as adjunctive anti-inflammatory and subsequently antiplatelet therapy
For high-risk or immunoglobulin-resistant disease, add corticosteroids, a further dose of immunoglobulin, or a TNF inhibitor such as infliximab
Perform serial echocardiography using body-surface-area-adjusted z-scores to detect and monitor coronary artery aneurysms
Tailor antithrombotic therapy to coronary findings, adding anticoagulation for large aneurysms
Maintain long-term cardiology follow-up with multidisciplinary paediatric rheumatology and cardiology care
Keep a low threshold to treat infants with prolonged fever and incomplete criteria given their high aneurysm risk
